intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis with neurologic defects (SDCHCN) is caused by mutation in the SLC2A1 gene (138140) on chromosome 1p34.2.

paragraphs.text: Stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis with neurologic defects is a rare form of stomatocytosis. Its features are a cold-induced red cell cation leak, hemolytic anemia and hepatosplenomegaly, together with cataracts, seizures, mental retardation and movement disorder (Flatt et al., 2011). Bawazir et al. (2012) described an infant with the disorder whose red cells lost potassium in a temperature-dependent way, which produced pseudohyperkalemia.

paragraphs.text: Fricke et al. (2004) described cases of stomatin-deficient hereditary stomatocytosis that differed in how the passive K+ leak depended on temperature. In 3 cases the leak followed a simple monotonic temperature dependence. In the other 2 cases the leak was lowest at around 20 to 25 degrees C, and the cells were extremely leaky at 0 degrees C, giving the phenotype known as cryohydrocytosis. The authors stated that these were the only 2 known cases of stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis. Both patients had a congenital syndrome of mental retardation, seizures, cataracts and massive hepatosplenomegaly. Fricke et al. (2004) suggested that this probably defined a new haemato-neurologic syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Bawazir et al. (2012) reported an infant who presented with erratic hyperkalemia, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, anemia, hepatic dysfunction and microcephaly. Seizures developed later, and developmental milestones were delayed. Magnetic resonance imaging and CT scans of the brain showed multiple abnormalities, including periventricular calcification. Visual impairment resulted from both cataracts and retinal dysfunction. The authors noted that this was the fourth pedigree described with the syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Lande et al. (1982) used SDS gel electrophoresis to separate erythrocyte membrane band 7 into 3 components of about 30, 28 and 26 kD. The 28-kD component was decreased in a patient with hereditary stomatocytosis and in a patient with cryohydrocytosis. On 2-dimensional electrophoresis, the 28-kD component separated into 2 proteins, 22 x 8 and 60 x 8. Protein 22 x 8 was completely absent in both patients, whereas 60 x 8 was present as usual.

paragraphs.text: In an infant with SDCHCN, Bawazir et al. (2012) identified a trinucleotide deletion in the SLC2A1 gene that deletes isoleucine-435 or isoleucine-436 of GLUT1. The infant had pseudohyperkalemia, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, anemia, hemolysis, hepatic dysfunction and microcephaly. Seizures and developmental delay followed, along with periventricular calcification, cataracts and retinal dysfunction. The proband's red cells were extremely leaky to cations and lost potassium in a temperature-dependent way.
